propositions.label: AI raises financial-stability risks through correlated behaviour
propositions.criterion: Widespread use of similar AI or machine-learning models, data or techniques by financial firms could make their decisions more alike (herding, uniformity, correlated trading or lending), which could amplify shocks, procyclicality or market volatility.

propositions.label: Reliance on a few AI providers creates concentration risk
propositions.criterion: Dependence of many financial firms on a small number of providers of AI models, data, cloud computing or related services creates concentration or third-party risk for the financial system, such that the failure or disruption of one provider could affect many firms at once.

propositions.label: AI increases cyber, fraud and operational risks in finance
propositions.criterion: AI, including generative AI, increases the capabilities available for cyberattacks, fraud, impersonation (such as deepfakes) or market manipulation against financial firms, customers or markets, or adds operational risks that financial authorities should take into account.

propositions.label: The opacity of AI models complicates risk management and supervision
propositions.criterion: The limited explainability or interpretability of AI or machine-learning models (the 'black box' problem) makes it harder for financial firms to manage their risks, or for supervisors to assess them or hold firms accountable.

propositions.label: AI can improve nowcasting and policy analysis
propositions.criterion: Machine-learning or AI techniques can improve nowcasting, forecasting, the processing of large or unstructured data, or other economic and policy analysis used by central banks.

propositions.label: AI's economic effects matter for monetary policy
propositions.criterion: The effects of AI on productivity, labour markets, prices, investment or the neutral rate of interest are relevant to the conduct of monetary policy, so that central banks need to assess or respond to them.

propositions.label: AI agents will change payment flows
propositions.criterion: AI agents acting for people or firms will or could initiate, negotiate or execute payments and transactions, changing how payments are made or the demands placed on payment systems.

propositions.label: AI agents' transactions bear on tokenised money and stablecoins
propositions.criterion: Transactions initiated by AI agents would use, require or favour programmable or tokenised forms of money, stablecoins or tokenised deposits, or AI would interact with such forms of money in ways that matter for the monetary system.

propositions.label: Supervisors should use AI
propositions.criterion: Financial supervisors or regulators can, or should, use AI or machine-learning tools (supervisory technology, 'suptech') to carry out supervision, including detecting misconduct, money laundering or emerging risks.

propositions.label: AI can improve financial firms' risk management
propositions.criterion: AI or machine-learning models can improve financial firms' measurement or management of risk, such as credit assessment, fraud detection, anti-money-laundering controls or market-risk modelling.

propositions.label: Central banks need to build their own AI capacity
propositions.criterion: Central banks need to invest in their own AI capabilities (data, computing, skills or staff), or to cooperate or pool resources with other central banks, to make use of AI or keep pace with its adoption.

propositions.label: Existing financial rules broadly cover AI
propositions.criterion: Existing financial regulatory and supervisory frameworks (for example technology-neutral rules on model risk, governance, outsourcing or consumer protection) broadly apply to the use of AI by financial firms, so that AI does not, or does not yet, require a separate regulatory framework.
propositions.pairedWith: A text holding that existing frameworks are insufficient and new AI-specific rules are needed contests U12.

records.statement: In a speech of 25 January 2017, Mark Carney, Governor of the Bank of England and Chair of the Financial Stability Board, said that robo-advice and risk management algorithms in wholesale banking and markets may lead to excess volatility or pro-cyclicality through herding, particularly if the algorithms are highly correlated.
records.missing: The passage concerns algorithms and robo-advice generally; it does not attribute the herding risk to AI or machine-learning models, data or techniques.
records.qualification: The passage speaks of algorithms in general, within a speech on fintech; it does not name AI or machine learning as the source of the correlation. The speech elsewhere lists “innovations in machine learning” among enabling technologies. A statement of a possible risk, not evidence that it has materialised.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 11), section on systemic risks of fintech
evidence.passage: In wholesale banking and markets, robo-advice and risk management algorithms may lead to excess volatility or increase pro-cyclicality as a result of herding, particularly if the underlying algorithms are overly sensitive to price movements or highly correlated.

records.statement: In remarks of 13 April 2017, Haruhiko Kuroda, Governor of the Bank of Japan, said that there are concerns that high-frequency and algorithmic trading may increase market volatility, especially if massive trading is based on a similar algorithm, and that applying AI and big data analytics to such trading might intensify these effects.
records.qualification: A conditional statement in opening remarks: the concern about similar algorithms is reported as one side of an argument, and the speaker's own claim is that AI 'might intensify' it. Not evidence that such effects occurred; the remarks do not state a Bank of Japan position.

evidence.locator: Section on new issues for market stakeholders and policymakers, paragraph beginning 'High-frequency trading (HFT) and algorithmic trading'
evidence.passage: At the same time, there are also concerns that HFT and algorithmic trading may increase market volatility, especially if massive trading is based on a similar algorithm
As such, the application of AI and big data analytics to HFT and algorithmic trading might intensify these negative impacts.

records.statement: The FSB report of 27 June 2017 on financial stability implications from FinTech states that social trading and robo-advice could show greater herding behaviour than traditional portfolio allocation if risk models are highly correlated through reliance on similar algorithms, and notes that it found no empirical evidence so far of convergence of robo-advisors’ algorithms or portfolios.
records.missing: The passage does not name AI or machine-learning models; it concerns robo-advice and social trading algorithms generally.
records.qualification: The passage concerns robo-advice and social trading algorithms; it does not name AI or machine learning (the report’s glossary says robo-advisors "can also include machine learning"). Recorded as context to the November 2017 articulation.

evidence.locator: Section 3 (financial stability risks), PDF p. 24 (printed p. 20)
evidence.passage: Social trading and robo-advice could potentially exhibit greater herding behaviour than traditional portfolio allocation methods – for example, if risk models are highly correlated due to reliance on similar algorithms – thereby potentially increasing the amplitude of swings in asset prices.
we found no empirical evidence so far on convergence of robo-advisors’ algorithms or portfolios.

records.statement: The FSB report of 1 November 2017 on artificial intelligence and machine learning in financial services states that if many market participants use similar AI and machine-learning programmes, the resulting correlated risks may entail financial stability risks and, as with any herding behaviour, could amplify financial shocks.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. The report states that there was no evidence of this occurring at the time and frames it as a possibility with greater adoption; its analysis is described as preliminary.

evidence.passage: if many market participants come to use similar AI and machine learning programmes in areas such as credit scoring or financial market activities, the consequent correlated risks may entail financial stability risks.

While there is no evidence of this occurring to date, this could become relevant with greater adoption of such trading strategies. As with any herding behaviour in the market, this has the potential to amplify financial shocks.

evidence.locator: Section 5.3 "Networks and interconnectedness", PDF p. 35 (printed p. 31)
evidence.passage: If a critical segment of financial institutions rely on the same data sources and algorithmic strategies, then under certain market conditions a shock to those data sources … could affect that segment as if it were a single node.

records.statement: In the IMF Departmental Paper of 22 October 2021, IMF staff authors El Bachir Boukherouaa, Khaled AlAjmi, Jose Deodoro, Aquiles Farias and Rangachary Ravikumar write that concentration of third-party AI/ML algorithm providers could drive greater homogeneity in risk assessments and credit decisions, with a risk of uniformity (herding), and that widespread AI/ML use could increase procyclicality.
records.qualification: A statement of what the text says, not evidence that the risk has materialised or that any authority has adopted a policy. A staff paper attributed to its authors.

evidence.locator: Chapter 3, section F "Impact on Financial Stability", second bullet (HTML)
evidence.passage: The concentration of third-party AI/ML algorithm providers could drive greater homogeneity in risk assessments and credit decisions in the financial sector, which, coupled with rising interconnectedness, could create the conditions for a buildup of systemic risks.
The widespread use of AI/ML could potentially increase procyclicality of financial conditions.

records.statement: The People's Bank of China's FinTech Development Plan 2022–2025, issued by notice of 29 December 2021, lists the herding effect (羊群效应), together with the algorithmic black box and algorithmic discrimination, among problems that financial institutions are to guard against through stress testing, simulation and parameter tuning.
records.missing: The passage names 羊群效应 (herding effect) as an algorithm problem to be prevented but does not state the mechanism (similar models or data making decisions alike) or that it could amplify shocks or volatility.
records.qualification: A planning document's task list in Chinese; the English rendering is a paraphrase. It records that the plan names the problem, not that herding has occurred or that measures were implemented.

evidence.locator: Attachment, chapter on tasks, item （二十四）筑牢金融与科技风险防火墙
evidence.passage: 通过临界测试、仿真模拟、参数调优等方式着力防范算法黑盒、羊群效应、算法歧视等问题，提升算法可解释性、透明性、公平性和安全性。
evidence.note: English paraphrase: through critical testing, simulation and parameter tuning, guard against problems such as the algorithmic black box, the herding effect and algorithmic discrimination, and raise the explainability, transparency, fairness and security of algorithms.

records.statement: The Basel Committee's newsletter of 16 March 2022 on AI and machine learning states that its continuing discussions will cover the potential implications of broader usage of AI/ML models for the resilience of individual banks and for financial stability.
records.missing: Names financial stability as an area for analysis but states no mechanism of correlated or herding behaviour.
records.qualification: The newsletter states it is for information only and is not supervisory guidance.

evidence.locator: Third of the three areas listed for continuing discussions
evidence.passage: The third area named for continuing discussions is the potential implications of broader usage of AI/ML models for the resilience of individual banks and, more broadly, for financial stability.

records.statement: The Bank of England (including the PRA) and the Financial Conduct Authority state in Discussion Paper DP5/22 of 11 October 2022 that AI models may become correlated in subtle ways and add to risks of herding or procyclical behaviour in market stress, and that uniformity across firms’ models could amplify procyclical behaviour.
records.qualification: A discussion paper inviting responses; it states possible risks and does not record that herding from AI has occurred or adopt a policy.

evidence.passage: models may become correlated in subtle ways and add to risks of herding, or procyclical behaviour at times of market stress.
algorithms may result in uniformity across models and approaches at multiple firms, which could amplify procyclical behaviour and lead to herding in certain use cases, such as algorithmic trading.

records.statement: In a keynote speech of 17 April 2024, Pablo Hernández de Cos, then Chair of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision and Governor of the Bank of Spain, said that AI/ML models have yet to be seen across a full financial cycle and could, left unchecked, potentially amplify future banking crises.
records.missing: The retrieved passage names no mechanism of similar models, data or techniques making firms' decisions alike; only the opening of the speech was retrieved, and the full text may say more.
records.qualification: The speaker's own views under his disclaimer. Recorded from the opening paragraphs published on the BIS page only.

evidence.locator: BIS page, paragraph beginning 'My main message is'
evidence.passage: Left unchecked, such models could potentially amplify future banking crises.

records.statement: A special feature of the ECB’s Financial Stability Review of May 2024, prepared by Georg Leitner, Jaspal Singh, Anton van der Kraaij and Balázs Zsámboki, states that widespread AI adoption may harbour the potential for increased herding behaviour and market correlation, and that AI could lead to distorted asset prices, increased correlation, herding or bubbles.
records.qualification: A staff-prepared special feature published in the Financial Stability Review; the page carries no statement that it is the Governing Council’s view. It describes channels and conditions (technological penetration and supplier concentration), not observed herding.

evidence.passage: widespread AI adoption may harbour the potential for increased herding behaviour and market correlation.
As a result, AI may make market participants’ conclusions systematically biased, leading to distorted asset prices, increased correlation, herding behaviour or bubbles.

records.statement: The BIS Annual Economic Report 2024 (chapter III) states that the behaviour of financial institutions using the same algorithms could amplify procyclicality and market volatility by exacerbating herding, liquidity hoarding, runs and fire sales.

time.note: Chapter released 25 June 2024 according to the BIS press release.

records.qualification: It states a possible risk; it does not report observed herding.
